edition.notes: Wilson expands the manuscript's contractions, so his text compares directly with a modern missal's orthography. The printed page carries marginal sigla (R. S., Gerb., Pam., Men., Bml.) between the words of the prayers; an optical text layer interleaves those sigla with the Latin and they must be recognised as intrusions rather than readings.
edition.publication: Oxford: at the Clarendon Press, 1894. Edited by Henry Austin Wilson from Vatican, Reg. lat. 316, with the readings of the eighth-century Gelasians in the margins and apparatus.
edition.title: The Gelasian Sacramentary: Liber sacramentorum Romanae ecclesiae, edited with introduction, critical notes and appendix by H. A. Wilson

passages.context: The seventh of the sixteen unassigned Sunday masses of Book III (which opens at Wilson p. 224). It carries, as one mass-set, the three orations of the 1962 Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost: the collect Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, qui abundantia pietatis tuae (Wilson prints adiicias; his apparatus records the manuscript's habundantiam and Pamelius' oratione); a second collect, Omnipotens sempiterne Deus, a quo sola sancta desideria; the secret Respice, Domine, quaesumus, nostram propitius servitutem with no et before the second sit and with the apparatus note that the genitive fragilitatis is the reading of the manuscript and the Frankish witnesses against the Leonine and Pamelian dative fragilitati; and the postcommunion Sentiamus, Domine, quaesumus in the older Domine-first word order, with the notes that the manuscript reads perceptionem and that the Leonine inserts de. Wilson's footnote 1 assigns this missa in the Rheinau and St-Gall Gelasians and Gerbert to the thirteenth Sunday after Pentecost and points to the twelfth Sunday in Pamelius. The exact remote artifact bytes were re-fetched and their SHA-256 matched this record before reading.

work.author: Catholic Church
work.description: The oldest surviving ordered Roman sacramentary, in three books, copied in Gaul about the middle of the eighth century from a Roman book of the seventh. Its attribution to Gelasius I is traditional and not maintained. It is the principal witness for a large part of the Roman oration repertory that the twentieth-century reform drew on.
work.title: Liber sacramentorum Romanae aeclesiae ordinis anni circuli
